outcomes.title: [AI DRAFT] Explain a function from the workspace

args.reason: Inspect src/timing.js and briefly compare debounce with throttling.

outcomes.prose:
`debounce(fn, wait)` delays calling `fn` until no new call has occurred for `wait` milliseconds. Each call resets the timer, so only the final call in a burst runs.

Use it when you care about the completed action, such as:

- Search suggestions after the user stops typing
- Saving after edits pause
- Handling window resize after resizing ends

Use throttling when you need regular updates during continuous activity, such as scrolling or pointer movement.

outcomes.title: [AI DRAFT] Explain a function from the workspace
outcomes.prose:
**What it does:** `debounce(fn, wait)` in `src/timing.js` returns a wrapped version of `fn`. Each call to the wrapper cancels the pending timer and starts a new `wait` ms timer. `fn` runs only after `wait` ms pass with no new calls. It runs once, with the arguments from the last call.

Limitations of this version:
- It is trailing-edge only, so there is no immediate first call.
- It has no `cancel` or `flush`.
- It doesn't preserve `this`, because it uses an arrow function.
- It returns nothing, so you can't get `fn`'s result.

**Debounce vs. throttle:**
- **Debounce** waits until the activity stops, then fires once. Use it when only the final value matters:
  - search-as-you-type requests
  - autosaving after the user stops editing
  - validating a field after typing
  - recomputing layout after a window resize ends
- **Throttle** fires at most once per interval while the activity continues. Use it when you need regular updates during the activity:
  - scroll or drag handlers
  - mousemove tracking
  - progress reporting
  - rate-limiting API calls

A continuous stream of events never lets a debounced function fire until the stream pauses. If you need updates during the stream, use throttle.

outcomes.title: [AI DRAFT] A one-line question gets a one-line answer
outcomes.prose:
HTTP 418 is "I'm a teapot". It comes from RFC 2324, the Hyper Text Coffee Pot Control Protocol, an April Fools' joke from 1998. A teapot returns it when it's asked to brew coffee, because it can't.

Some servers still use it as an Easter egg. Others use it to turn away unwanted requests, such as bots. It isn't meant for real use, and the status code is reserved so that it doesn't get reassigned.
